speakeroldname: Mr. John N. Turner (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
subtopic: OWNERSHIP OF OFFSHORE MINERAL RIGHTS, B.C.
speechtext:
1. At the meeting in October last of the Prime Minister and the provincial premiers, the question of conflicting claims with regard to jurisdiction over offshore mineral rights, including oil and minerals off the coast of British Columbia, was raised and discussed. This was the first occasion in which this question was raised formally as a subject for discussion at a federal-provincial conference and it was not expected that any decisions would be reached

at that time. At the conclusion of the discussion of this matter the Prime Minister indicated that the federal government would shortly be in touch with the provinces so that steps might be taken to move to an early definition of the respective positions of the federal government and the provincial governments.
2. At the federal-provincial conference the federal government proposed to the provinces that a reference be taken to the Supreme Court of Canada so that the question of jurisdiction could be settled. It was also proposed that the terms of the reference to the supreme court should be on an agreed basis with the provinces if possible and that some arrangements be entered into between the federal government and the provincial governments to ensure that there would be no interference with resource development while consideration by the Supreme Court of Canada takes place.

Mr. Chairman, if there are no other questions, perhaps I might reply briefly to the questions raised mainly by the hon. member for Edmonton West.
In respect of the desirability of national emergency measures exercises, it is of course understood that there has not been such an exercise on a national scale for a number of years. One was projected for a couple of years ago but in fact was not carried out. Those who were responsible for the preparation of that projected exercise did in fact derive a great deal of benefit from the preparation of it, and the emergency measures organization benefited from a review of its activities in this regard. Obviously that value is something less than the value to be derived from a full scale national exercise, but such an exercise would be much more expensive.
It is the view at this time of the emergency measures organization that rather than to attempt another national exercise at this juncture it would be better-this is what we are indeed planning to do-to have a cycle of exercises, as is normal in military training, starting at the municipal level, followed by the provincial level and finally followed by a full scale exercise at the federal level, involving all levels. This is the plan under which we are now operating.
In respect of the civil defence college, I should like to advise the hon. member that the average intake now is approximately 80 students per course. The program includes a basic orientation course for federal employees, specialists courses for departments such as the Department of National Health and Welfare and the Department of Agriculture. It also includes emergency supply planning, technical courses on radiation monitoring and fallout protection, national survival organization and planning, and an operations course for provincial and municipal civil defence workers who have previously received their basic training through a local civil defence training course.
In 1963 the college trained 2,866 planners and 1,453 planners so far in this current year, making a cumulative total to date of more than 33,700. It is evident that the college facilities are normally used to maximum capacity providing courses in both the French and 20220-618

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, this is an item which very frequently passes the house without much notice. I think this is rather unfortunate although I do not propose taking much time to discuss it today. The atomic energy control board, as I am sure the minister will confirm, performs a very important function in providing control over all the atomic energy activities that are going on in this country, so that the people are protected from the danger that can occur if something goes wrong with atomic energy research stations. Although the house frequently lets the atomic energy control board estimates go through without much consideration, I think it is important for us to recognize what the board does. It has a very important function to perform and over the years we have been singularly fortunate in Canada that we have not been unduly alarmed at any time or subjected to any danger from radioactive materials from any of our own establishments.
This good situation results from an absolutely first class piece of work on the part of the atomic energy control board. It has been chaired by various people, all of whom have carried out their duties efficiently. I thought I would draw the attention of the house to what my own experience was in working with the atomic energy control board and recommend commendation for the board for the work it is doing for the people of Canada. speakerposition: Minister of Industry; Minister of Defence Production
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am most appreciative of the kind remarks of the hon. member commending the work of the atomic energy control board. Needless to say, in this important field involving the regulation of the peaceful uses of atomic energy in Canada we have been fortunate in the high purpose, assiduity and perspicacity of the members of the atomic energy control board.
During the past year the board has considered applications for and issued some 1,117 licences covering the use of radioisotopes in Canada. It has issued some 172 permits covering dealings in other atomic energy materials and some 62 permits covering operations with fissile material. Mr. Chairman, I should like to ask two short questions of the minister. I read in a trade journal recently that there is some danger that the whole western world will be short of uranium oxide and other fissionable substances throughout the 1970's. I was wondering whether the commission might make a survey of the situation and advise other departments of the government whether in fact Canada is facing a shortage so that we might encourage the development of the industry which was doing very well a few years ago. If commercial ventures are not going to be allowed in the national parks, at least independent government teams could look for possible sources of uranium oxide in the parks so that if a shortage does develop in the 1970's we will not lack fissionable materials for our projects at Chalk River and other such places.

speakerposition: Minister of Industry; Minister of Defence Production
speechtext:
The hon. member will recall when last I spoke of Atomic Energy of Canada Limited, I did give an extensive review of the progress up to that time of the operations of the company. Perhaps I might try to bring the committee up to date briefly.
The heavy water moderated and cooled natural uranium fueled reactor system continues to dominate the Canadian nuclear scene. The successful operation of Canada's first nuclear power station, the 20,000 kilowatt nuclear power demonstration unit, coupled with the enthusiasm for the Canadian nuclear power system shown in many quarters internationally, fully vindicates those who first urged its development.
Canada's first full scale nuclear power station of 200,000 kilowatt output with its single reactor, generally known as CANDU, now being built by Atomic Energy of Canada Limited with the co-operati( n of the HydroElectric Power Commission of Ontario at Douglas Point, is expected to be completed in time for commercial operation in 1965 and at a cost that is not expected to exceed the budget figure of some $81.5 million. The preliminary design by Atomic Energy of Canada Limited of the nuclear system and by Ontario hydro of the conventional system of a one million kilowatt nuclear generating station employing two reactors has been completed and, as the committee is well aware, agreement has been reached between the government of Canada, the government of Ontario and Ontario hydro concerning the arrangements that will prevail in respect of the construction of such a station. I might emphasize that the decision to adopt this particular design and to employ Atomic Energy of Canada Limited as the designer has been made by Ontario hydro and it is Ontario

hydro not Atomic Energy of Canada Limited that will build this plant. In other words, Ontario hydro is using its normal procurement methods for this plant, rather than the special arrangements worked out for Douglas Point.
Atomic Energy of Canada Limited has always enjoyed a close relationship with Canadian industry. In response to an invitation by atomic energy, individual companies are seconding staff to atomic energy research and design locations to gain first hand knowledge and experience of the Canadian nuclear power system. Now that decision has been taken to proceed with the proposed new Ontario hydro station, it is expected that this type of liaison between atomic energy and industry will be accelerated. This procedure has the advantage of releasing atomic energy facilities for new and diversified projects, while giving industry an opportunity of being more closely integrated with the Canadian program.
The design of the 200,000 kilowatt nuclear generating station for India is proceeding at full speed and in full co-operation with atomic energy's power product group acting as nuclear consultants for the Indian department of atomic energy. Montreal Engineering Company Limited has signed a contract with the department of atomic energy of India for the design of the conventional part of the station and will act as consultant to that department in the construction of the station.
Negotiations are at present under way between Canadian General Electric Company Limited and the Pakistan atomic energy commission for the sale of a 132 megawatt nuclear power station of Canadian design to be located at Karachi. Elsewhere on the international scene it is safe to say that interest in the Canadian system is keen; so also is competition from other industrialized nations. But I am sure that an aggressive Canadian industry employing a very sharp pencil, and encouraged by A.E.C.L., should be able to look to markets abroad in the nuclear power field in the years immediately ahead.
Research, of course, is the lifeblood of Atomic Energy of Canada Limited. The Chalk River nuclear laboratories research team, a group with a world wide reputation for original work, continues to employ the excellent facilities located at Chalk River to their limit. While, of necessity, effort must be concentrated on research and development incidental to all aspects of the heavy water moderated and cooled reactor system in order to back up commitments made, A.E.C.L. is making the preliminary studies necessary to

the launching of a program for the development of a heavy water moderated, boiling light water cooled, natural uranium reactor system.
Construction of the Whiteshell nuclear research establishment in Manitoba is continuing on schedule. Four major buildings are now in use and some useful research work is at present under way.
Hon. members will be interested to learn that A.E.C.L. has now firm requirements for heavy water that exceed the 1,000 tons of production in the first five years of the operation of the plant in Nova Scotia being built by Deuterium of Canada Limited. A.E.C.L. has, on behalf of the government of Canada, undertaken to guarantee the sale of the first five years of production from this plant at the rate of 200 tons per year, starting July 1966.
The requirements of the Douglas Point generating station borrowed from the United States atomic energy commission, plus the requirements of the million kilowatt station recently announced for Ontario hydro, total about 1,150 tons. There are additional smaller amounts needed during this five year period to meet the Chalk River and Whiteshell research reactor requirements, which total about 35 tons. There is also a need for 150 tons for the 132 megawatt nuclear plant for Pakistan, if that project proceeds, and there are several other potential requirements that could total some hundreds of tons in the same period.
A.E.C.L. and other users will be exploring the possibility of further production in Canada, as it is now obvious that 200 tons per year will not meet Canadian requirements, and foreign sales appear to be considerable. If, during the 1970's, the heavy water moderated power reactors are developed to use boiling light water or light water steam for the coolant, the total requirements of heavy water for each plant will be reduced by about one fifth. However, at that time the rate of installation of these plants should be such that there will be an assured market for increased production, assuming of course that the price is competitive with other sources of supply.
Hon. members are familiar with the success that has been achieved by A.E.C.L.'s commercial products division in Ottawa. The products manufactured by this group find their way to purchasers in every comer of the globe. So great has been the increase in the volume of sales that A.E.C.L., in order to keep pace with the orders, has decided to
Supply-Defence Production construct a new building on the outskirts of this city.
I think this suffices to give a brief summary of progress to date of Atomic Energy of Canada Limited, and I would recommend that these estimates be passed by the committee.

I am not going into the intricacies of atomic energy because I know nothing about them, but on at least two or three occasions I asked the minister whether a decision has been reached by the atomic energy commission on the application of Ontario hydro for a definite site for the location of its nuclear power plant, more particularly in Fairport in Ontario county. Since he has already admitted that the application was received on September 8, and since two months have passed since then, I would like to know whether this site has been approved. If not, when does the minister think the commission might be able to give approval in order to expedite the construction of the plant?

speakerposition: Minister of Industry; Minister of Defence Production
speechtext:
I can hardly resist the temptation to point out to the hon. member that we have passed items 1 and 5. Consequently I cannot avail myself of the advice of Dr. Lawrence, who was here a few moments ago. However, I did discuss this point with him. Supply-Defence Production Once we know the site has been approved that will ease the minds of a lot of people.

speakerposition: Minister of Industry; Minister of Defence Production
speechtext: Well, if I may suggest so, there is no such thing as an appropriate site and an inappropriate site. It all depends on what you are going to do at any given site. What might be right and proper to do in a certain way on the shores of Hudson bay would be quite wrong to do downtown in Toronto, particularly in the nuclear field. It is not so much a question of approving the site as examining what Ontario hydro proposes to do, and how it proposes to do it in Fairport. I think I can say, without revealing anything I should not, that in relation to the initial proposals of Ontario hydro for the operation of this station the atomic energy control board made some counter-suggestions as to how it should be done. It is the interplay of suggestion and counter suggestion, looking toward the safety of the general public, which takes the time; it is not simply a case of saying yes or no to a site, but it is, rather, the making of decisions with regard to the technical aspects of what is to be done at a particular site.

I think it is only appropriate for me to have a few words to say when the estimates of Atomic Energy of Canada are being considered, particularly since one of the research establishments is located within my riding. I must say the people of Springfield are proud of this research centre which is located there. It has done a great deal to stimulate this part of the country. I think it is a most beautiful site for a most worthwhile project.
The former government set up a special committee of the House of Commons a few years ago to deal with research, and representatives of Atomic Energy of Canada Limited, Eldorado, Eldorado Aviation and the national research council appeared before it. At that time some of the controversy surrounding the type of reactor which Canada should be producing was brought into the open. I think a good deal of healthy discussion came out of that committee and I believe that to a large extent the stand taken by Atomic Energy of Canada has been vindicated and that the type of reactor which Canada is producing is practical and saleable. There are a number of questions I should like to address to the minister. Perhaps he could take note of them while I am speaking and provide me with some answers.
First, I wonder whether he could explain to me the manner in which housing is


financed at Whiteshell and how those houses are taken over by the residents. Are they rented, or are they bought? How much money is Atomic Energy putting into the townsite? Is Central Mortgage and Housing underwriting this expenditure?
The minister mentioned that Atomic Energy of Canada is considering the production of a different type of reactor, one which would be cooled by hot water or steam. He told the committee this would reduce the cost of some of our reactors and the amount of heavy water which would be required. There has been talk, also, of an organically cooled reactor. I should like the minister to tell us what is meant by an organically cooled reactor as well as by a hot water cooled reactor, and whether the use of such coolants would reduce the cost of the reactor. I should also like to know the effect of these developments upon the use of heavy water.
In the United States at the present time there is a great deal of talk about using nuclear reactors for the desalinization of ocean water. This is a pet project of President Johnson and, indeed, it will be brought up at the forthcoming meeting of NATO parliamentarians. As one of the leaders in the field of nuclear research, Canada should I believe be in a position to play an active part in the development of reactors which could be used for desalinization. I notice that invitations have gone out to 114 nations to attend an international symposium or saline water conversion to be held in October, 1965, and I am sure that Atomic Energy Limited must have some plan about attending this conference. Perhaps the minister could outline to us the action he intends to take in this regard. I notice also that at the present time a Montreal company has submitted a proposal for an 80 megawatt plant with a desalinization capacity of 14,000 cubic meters per day. I think this would be a combined power station and desalinization plant.
I mention this because it seems to me that the interest in desalinization among various nations of the world where there is a shortage of fresh water is such that it might provide a definite market for nuclear reactors produced in Canada. There is no doubt that United States companies will be bidding in this field and I should like to be assured that Atomic Energy of Canada is not dragging its heels in this regard but, rather, doing work which would put it in a position to tender for the supply of reactors to be used for desalinization. I realize that desaliniza-

tion is not of primary importance to Canada, because we are fortunate in having an ample supply of fresh water. But because of the limited market for these reactors and because the taxpayers of Canada are making such large amounts available for research to Atomic Energy of Canada Limited, we should not miss any opportunity to capitalize on overseas markets. Perhaps the minister could give us an answer in this regard.
I just want to say that relations between the town and Atomic Energy Limited are most cordial. The people in this town are somewhat above the average. I understand that the I.Q. of school children at Deep River is considerably above the average. I know there were some problems of administration at Deep River in the early days and I hope these difficulties will be avoided in Whiteshell. I trust a certain amount of autonomy will be granted to this town so that it will not be a company town, but rather an incorporated municipality as soon as a decision to let these people govern themselves is warranted. I hope also that this community in Manitoba, one which thousands of visitors will go to see and marvel at every year, will not become isolationist. I know there is a tendency among these people to keep to themselves. But I hope the public spirit and leadership which is evident among the people will be shared by the community at large. The former government chose a site in Manitoba for this research establishment in order to decentralize the operation at Chalk River which had grown to capacity. I think this decision was a proper one. I am glad the minister is following up the work which has been done and I trust the work being done at Whiteshell and Chalk River will in the years to come contribute to the advancement of Canada and of the world at large in the nuclear field.

The hon. gentleman said that Ontario hydro was building a new plant with the assistance of Atomic Energy Limited. I wonder whether the minister would tell us whether, as different contracts come up, private industry will be given every consideration in regard to them. Does the hon. gentleman feel that private industry today is playing a large enough part in the promotion of atomic energy and the construction of different plants in this country?

speakerposition: Minister of Industry; Minister of Defence Production
speechtext:
The hon. member for Springfield asked some questions about housing in connection with the Whiteshell reactor in Manitoba. These houses are financed by Atomic
Supply-Defence Production Energy of Canada Limited, who secure the necessary money to build them from the government under the heading of loans or advances. This money is borrowed from the government at commercial rates of interest. What about the amortization?

speakerposition: Minister of Industry; Minister of Defence Production
speechtext:
I cannot give this information offhand, Mr. Chairman. I suspect it is of the order of 30 years; the same kind of criteria used by central mortgage and housing. The hon. member also asked whether I would undertake a brief dissertation on organically cooled reactors. As the hon. member knows, in a reactor there is required a medium to control the flow of neutrons, known as a moderator, and another substance is required to carry the heat generated from the interior of the reactor to a source where the heat energy can be used. In the case of the CANDU reactor, heavy water is used both as a moderator to control the flow of neutrons and also as a coolant to carry the heat generated by fission from the interior of the reactor to a spot where it can be transformed from heat energy to mechanical energy. Heavy water is an expensive item in itself- at the present time costing the Canadian government some $20.50 a pound-and using it as a coolant can be expensive, in terms of leakages and losses of one sort or another which require replacement.
As a consequence, as I outlined in my opening remarks, Atomic Energy of Canada Limited is investigating the possibility of a system employing heavy water as a moderator-that is, continuing its employment as a moderator-but using as a coolant, or the medium for the transfer of heat from the reactor to the power generating system, boiling, light water, or ordinary boiling water- that is, ordinary water under considerable pressure, which will boil. Obviously the loss of this kind of water is not nearly so expensive to make up and replace. In addition to the possibilities of using heavy water as a moderator and boiling, light water as a coolant there are also some organic substances, organic liquids, whose values, advantages and disadvantages are currently planned for investigation at Whiteshell. This will be one of its main, initial preoccupations, namely the

investigation of organic coolants, together with inorganic water. As hon. members know, the reactor there has its future ahead of it rather than behind it, so what the results of these investigations will be I of course cannot now say.
The hon. member also asked whether we would be participating in a 114-nation symposium next year on the use of nuclear energy for desalination, if I understood the question correctly. The answer to this question is yes, of course we will be. But I might say, in relation to the desalination program generally-and this is also to some degree an answer to the question asked by the hon. member for Peterborough-that Atomic Energy of Canada Limited is in the business of research in the field of nuclear energy and also in design, but is not in-and indeed in my view should not get into-the business of manufacturing and selling nuclear reactors. The function of A.E.C.L. up to the present has been-and I suggest should continue to be for the future-to produce ideas which it endeavours to farm out to manufacturing industry in Canada, and let industry make use of their capacities, their talents, to refine, to manufacture and to sell the reactors and the components of the reactors in this particular field.
We have potential manufacturers of reactors in Canada. In my opening remarks I pointed out that the government of Pakistan and Canadian General Electric were now negotiating for a contract for the manufacture and delivery, on a turnkey basis, in Karachi of a reactor. The role of Atomic Energy of Canada in this matter is to act as adviser, but the negotiator, the contractor who will manufacture, deliver and guarantee the apparatus will not be Atomic Energy of Canada; it will be Canadian General Electric. Similarly in the desalination field, the reactors required for heat generation in what is, in effect, a massive distillation process, will be their manufacture and their sale; in other words, the manufacture and sale will be the responsibility of manufacturing industry in Canada, rather than of Atomic Energy of Canada Limited. Consequently our role at the conference to which the hon. member made reference will be that of technical expert or technical adviser, rather than a manufacturer interested in sales.
The hon. member also had some kind things to say about the relationship between the scientific community at Whiteshell and the local community. As the hon. member well knows, one of the reasons for choosing the


site at which the Whiteshell reactor, or the Whiteshell research station is being put up is the proximity of the University of Manitoba. It was because it was intended that there should be the closest possible relationship between the scientific community of Whiteshell and the university communities, not only of Manitoba but of the other provinces as well, that this site was chosen. It is certainly the object of A.E.C.L.-as indeed it is the object of the government-that there should be no tendency to what I think the hon. gentleman referred to as isolationism, of which I do not think there has been any evidence so far.

Mr. Chairman, I am prompted to say what I want to say now by the fact that the minister said the product with which we are concerned-I think I quote his words correctly-has to look for markets abroad and has to find its way to purchasers in every corner of the globe. If this is true, it seems to me it is about time we began to seriously consider looking for a different system of measurement than the one we use today. Of course I mean the metric system of measurement. Dr. Howlett, who is the director of applied physics at the national research council, says that a real crisis confronts the users of the English system.

Mr. Chairman, perhaps I may be allowed to continue what I began at the wrong place a moment ago. It seems to me that this is a favourable time at which to open the issue as to whether we should seriously consider taking the first steps toward introducing a metric system in this country. As Dr. Howlett pointed out, and as I quoted

a moment ago, it is a matter of grave concern that Canada is not readying for the switch.
I think everyone in this country realizes that it will be a very difficult thing to do, and it will require a long period of time to make the proper preparations to do this with the least possible disruption to the country. Consequently I think we should begin to take these first steps.
I am prompted to say this by my experience with measurement, although purely academic, for a great many years. I know of the difficulties that students in this country have in handling our system, and I know of the lack of difficulty and the simplicity of the metric system when it is applied in the scientific field, including chemistry and physics. It seems to me that even if we begin to make preparation for this move we would not only be assisting our students, who find themselves in the world today facing extremely heavy competition in the field of science from every other country of the world, but also assisting those who are trying to capture markets outside this country.
I should like to point out that some 90 per cent of the world's population today uses the metric system and that 27 countries in Europe, the Soviet union, China, Japan and India, where we are interested in selling atomic projects, central and South America all use the metric system. In fact as the years go by Canada becomes an anachronism in this sense. We are becoming old hat when it comes to working with a modern system of measurement. This being so, are we making preparation for what I consider to be an inevitable change? We are handicapping our position in world markets if we do not make this change. We are handicapping our young people educationally if we do not make this change, and we are certainly going to handicap the consumers of this country by not making the change.
One can go into a supermarket to purchase something and find four or five different sized cans, each with a different price. If we used the metric system I am sure that many producers of goods would find it impossible to confuse the consumer as they do today. I suggest it is time that we began to consider making this change.

Great Britain is in fact changing its outmoded system of monetary measurement, and I think it would not be so stubborn as to refuse to change the other system.

Mr. Chairman, as I make my very brief remarks under this heading I should like to thank the minister for his courtesy and promptness in answering the number of questions I have placed on the order paper during the past several weeks relating to research grants.
Leading into my brief remarks this afternoon, Mr. Chairman, perhaps I should say that while most people of this day and age recognize that we here in Canada are privileged to live in a prosperous country, most responsible political leaders on all sides of this house recognize that we are still facing a basic challenge. I know the minister in another department of government is aware of this challenge in respect of general and regional poverty. I think we can also be thankful that in this day and age we do not meet poverty with old fashioned demagoguery, but by action. Here in the federal sphere of government, while we have not met with the provinces and planned priorities in the social action and economic fields, Canadian governmental leaders in the federal and provincial fields recognize that education stands high on our list of priorities.
I shall now come to my point. In fighting regional and general poverty the federal government has a keen leading role to play in encouraging what I have often termed individual and national excellence. The research council has a great role to play in encouraging basic research in Canada. I thought this would be an opportune time for the minister to make a very brief statement based on my general remarks.
At this particular time in our nation's history many university leaders are conducting symposiums to discuss the pros and cons of what is becoming known as the brain drain.
9768	HOUSE OF
Supply-Defence Production Some people think there is a serious brain drain of scientists from Canada. Others are not sure if there really is such a drain, while yet others recognize there is one but feel it is not as serious as it might be. In general terms there is a debate going on in the nation today relating to what people loosely and generally call a brain drain.
I know the minister will report to us at a future date on the many findings of the research secretariat, but I for one, without going into great detail, feel that if individual and national excellence is to be encouraged here in Canada, as we fight poverty with facts and not with slogans, and if we are really going to play a role in doing this, we have got to pay much more attention to encouraging basic research here in Canada, and this is going to cost the federal government a lot more money. I do not know whether these figures are correct or in exact detail, or on what they are based, but I have heard time and time again this coined expression expressed publicly, that while Canada spends $1 per scientist, the United Kingdom spends $3 and the United States spends $10 to $15. Perhaps the minister and his officials will wish to comment on these statistics I have put forward.
Prime Minister Wilson in his recently concluded campaign in the United Kingdom stressed that in his country, in order to get the economy moving forward in a realistic way, and in order to meet the basic challenge of poverty, he recognized the vital role as does President Johnson-that the government must play in increasing assistance to basic research. I should like to ask the minister to make some general statement at this time relating to his opinion about the causes of the brain drain of scientists from Canada to other countries, the extent of its seriousness and what positive policies the federal government now contemplates to encourage more Canadian scientists to stay in Canada, as we are attempting to encourage, through the federal government, individual and national excellence. This is something I feel we must do if we are going to really fight regional and general poverty.
As I said at the outset, I have put many questions relating to medical research matters on the order paper and I should like to thank the minister for his helpful answers and cooperation in this regard. It has been said over the last few months that we are about to face a critical shortage of doctors in Canada and that we must have more doctors in training if we are going to have the same
[Mr. GrafTtey.l

standards of medical care in 1970 as we have today. We have been warned time and time again not only in the Hall report but by other responsible individuals that unless we meet the challenge immediately we are going to be faced sooner rather than later with a critical shortage of doctors and dentists in Canada.
With assistance from various departments of government I have tried to get information in this regard. The Canadian universities foundation is carrying out a pilot research project in Ontario alone to find out how many applicants to study medicine were refused admission to medical schools this year. The initial figures are misleading because one student may have made four or five applications, but has only been accepted by one medical school, and yet the three or four refusals appear in the statistics. The Canadian universities foundation is doing important work in having individuals on their staff trying to get the true picture in this regard from the universities, but no matter what their findings may be I think we are all agreed that in the future, as we have learned from the Hall report and other sources, we are going to have to build more medical schools.
I should like to get to the point we are discussing under the particular item relating to grants for medical research. It seems to me that the federal government is going to have to play a much greater role in the future if we are going to keep our medical research scientists in Canada at more properly staffed medical schools. I should like the minister to outline the problem generally as he sees it at the present time. I know that nobody, including the medical research council, can always get exactly what it asks for. However, I feel it must be emphasized that if we are going to have more medical schools we will also have to have more medical schools doing more important research projects, which is going to involve a greater degree of assistance on the part of the federal authorities.
I know it is impossible to do justice to a subject of this nature in the time at our disposal. I also recognize that the minister is going to report on the findings of the research secretariat at a future date, but I hope he will find it opportune at the present time to give the committee a general outline of government policies intended to increase assistance for medical research in particular and industrial research in general, in order that we

can keep more Canadian scientists doing their work in Canada.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to say a tew words along the same lines with regard to medical research. In looking over the estimates for the last 10 years I notice that the budget of the national research council has increased from $14,794,367 in 1954-55 to $47,101,571 in 1963-64. This is quite a substantial increase. I think it is very well merited and perhaps reflects somewhat the interest that is being shown in research throughout Canada.
In the year 1963-64 $5,100,000 was allocated to medical research out of the over $47 million spent by the national research council. My beef, and it is one I have brought up in the house before, is that the amount of money allocated to dental research, which would be included of course in the figure I have given for medical research, bears no relationship whatsoever to the relationship of dentistry to medicine in our communities. The relationship between the amount spent on dentistry and the amount spent on medicine by the average person is far different from the relationship of the amount of money spent on dental research to that spent on medical research. I believe that only 1 to 2 per cent of the money spent on medical research is allocated to dentistry.
I am making this point for a very valid reason in that dental diseases are almost universal and yet are largely preventable. So it is a most deplorable situation when the community as a whole neglects to try to do something about dental diseases, which no doubt could be largely prevented if certain public health measures were followed and if further research were carried on.
My plea is that the national research council look into the matter to see if more money cannot be allocated to dental research. Perhaps the minister could give me an answer on that point. I know one answer is that it is pretty difficult to get anybody to do this type of research. Last year $31,953 was allocated for fellowships for dental research and $165,500, I believe, was allocated by way of grants for dental research projects, but all the money allocated in the last 10 years for dental research comes to less than $1 million, which is not even 20 per cent of the amount of money allocated for medical research last year alone.
I think there is a very great discrepancy here. I am not placing the blame solely on the minister or the national research council. I think that the bulk of the blame falls on
Supply-Defence Production the Minister of National Health and Welfare and the officials of that department, but I certainly should like to see the national research council allocate more of its budget for dental research and I would hope that this would be done in the future.

speakerposition: Minister of Industry; Minister of Defence Production
speechtext:
Clearly, Mr. Chairman, our research activities which are devoted to the improvement of efficiency and overcoming unnecessary slowness have now uncovered a new field for examination. Perhaps we could have a look to see if we could devise some way of stopping this slowdown.
The hon. member for Kindersley suggested that something should be done concerning the adoption of the metric system by Canada. I think the parliamentary secretary made the point fairly clearly that Canada cannot adopt the metric system unilaterally. Indeed, Canada cannot take very large steps toward the introduction of such a system as long as our largest buyer, the United States, is not taking
9770	HOUSE OF
Supply-Defence Production comparable steps in the same direction. However, preparations are being made looking toward this being achieved. As the hon. member will be well aware, in very large areas of the scientific community the metric system is the standard of measurement, not only in respect of weight and volume but also of length. This, of course, has extended into the schools now. When I was a boy, which was relatively few years ago, the metric system was unknown at the school I attended. We were satisfied with the English system of measurement. I understand now from my children, however, the metric system occupies as important a place as the English system of measurement in our schools today. This is extending, then, through the educational system some preparation for the adoption of the system.
As the pamphlet read to the committee by the hon. gentleman indicates, there is an awareness of this problem and a willingness to do something about it on the part of the national research council and its staff. I, myself, periodically in speeches exhort Canadian industry to prepare itself to meet the great markets of the world outside North America and to recognize that they are liable to have to sell their products under the metric rather than the English system of measurement. The changeover does call for a very substantial investment in both measuring equipment and manufacturing equipment. Perhaps one of the things we should be doing is giving some thought to the development or evolution of machinery which will be able to measure with equal facility in either the metric or English system. Some preliminary thought has been given to this. I believe the hon. member has raised a valid point and thought should be given to this. Preparations should be made. I should like to reassure him that thought has and is being given and preparations are being made. However, this is not something which is likely, nor indeed could, happen overnight.
The hon. member for Springfield, taking the easiest part of the task first, made the observation that in his view the amount of money devoted to dental research, as a proportion of the total amount devoted to medical research, was too small. I am not quite sure how one should divide up either the organs of the body or the ailments of the body and apportion the amount of money devoted to their investigation. I can tell him, however, that I have had representations from those interested in pediatrics who make exactly the same suggestion, that the amount of 

money devoted to the ailments of children is too small; that more is needed. Those who are interested in communicable diseases are of the view that too small a proportion of the total amount of money going to medical research is devoted to this series of ailments from which we suffer from time to time.
What do you think?

speakerposition: Minister of Industry; Minister of Defence Production
speechtext:
I have no answer as to what are the right proportions. I am told by the medical research council that where they can find high quality fellows in any medical field, including dentistry, they are only too glad to support them. In fact, the big problem in this area is to find competent, high quality people to support rather than trying to deny funds to deserving research fellows. The same is equally true in connection with applications for equipment grants in respect of medical research. Where there are deserving, high quality research projects, with what appears to be a useful potential, these are supported.
The hon. member may have noted that in the period from 1959-60, to date, the funds allocated to the medical research council have risen from some $2 million at an annual rate to a figure in 1964-65 of close to $7 million. This represents a growth factor of three during that period.
The medical research council, and indeed the national research council, are fully alive to the needs for increased research effort in our research community in this country, both for the work it can produce and the support research produces for the teaching apparatus in Canada. As a consequence, they are pressing the government which, in turn, is in agreement with this philosophy, to have increases almost on an annual basis in the amount of funds allocated for fundamental research in both the field of natural science and the field of medicine.
If the hon. gentleman has any influence in the dental community, I hope he will be able to urge them to bring forward high class applicants who would be interested in undertaking research in the dental field. If this can be done, I do not think there will be a refusal on the grounds of a lack of funds.
The hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi really invited me to survey the whole field of research, not only to survey it but also produce justification for it. This is a rather tall order. Perhaps I could briefly say that, in respect of medical research, what I have just said to the hon. member for Springfield has some relevance. The total amount devoted to medical research has risen by about the

same factor of three during this period 195960 to date. Here again the shortage, if any there be, is of qualified people rather than funds with which to support them. The hon. gentleman made some reference to the brain drain and of the investigations now being carried out to establish the real facts in connection with this situation, as distinct from what I believe to be some effort to try to extrapolate a few individual experiences and turn them into a condemnation of the whole system. The fact of the matter is that we have not too much factual data in this field. This is something I regret and something about which I hope I will be able to do something. We have got to have a great deal more in the way of background and factual information on which to base not only intelligent prognostications but also intelligent policies for the future. This, as the hon. gentleman is well aware, is one of the main reasons for the appointment of the scientific secretariat.

Hasn't the government a policy at the present time with regard to this? I may have misunderstood some of the things that were said during the campaigning and in this chamber since then, but I understood the government had a policy in relation to all these matters. I am now left with the impression that there is not any policy except "We will do some research and find out the facts and then get a policy."
The minister is really confusing us and I suggest to him we would appreciate something a little bit more positive, or else he should explain to us why we need facts and statistics now instead of a policy.

speakerposition: Minister of Industry; Minister of Defence Production
speechtext: I have not quite finished what I was going to say in reply to the hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi. Surely an intelligent policy should not be elaborated in the absence of facts? There are some people who advocate the construction of a policy on emotion, rumour or intuition, but in the field of science I do not think this should be the foundation upon which a policy is built. The hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi asked what we were doing about the so-called brain drain-

I would like the minister to explain to me what the national research council has been doing all these years and why we have had ministers responsible for scientific research all these years if now, in the fall of 1964, we find the minister coming forward saying we have not got a policy, that it is emotional and intuitive to enunciate a policy, and that he is waiting for the facts.
Supply-Defence Production What is the justification for the N.R.C. and all these fat reports we have had if we cannot get a statement on policy now? The only justification we have had is that each year the branch is getting a little bigger and so it could not be too bad.
The minister had better come off it and give us the government's policy on this whole question of science. The point raised by the hon. member for Springfield has been known to laymen such as myself who have only a nodding acquaintance with the dental profession. Yet the minister comes in and foists off a professional with the suggestion that some people have ideas and other people have other ideas. That is no answer. When the hell are we going to get some answers from the government and from people like the minister who has the responsibility? What bothers me is the casual slackness of coming with an item such as this and really dusting us off, saying he has to get some facts and figures.
Does the minister realize how aggravating and annoying this attitude is, especially when on other occasions, particularly when speeches are made outside the house, all the honours are given to the national research council and all these various academic people working in these fields? When we are given information in this chamber it is as though we were a bunch of dunces who could not understand it. I am going around in circles but I suggest the minister is going around in circles too.
At the very least the minister should give us an undertaking that some time within the next year, if this parliament survives, he will be able to come in and tell us the government's policy in the field of science and research, and fit into the picture somewhere the point raised about dentistry. He might even mention pediatrics, and give us some indication where the government is going.
Every damned ministry I know of has some kind of research or fact finding program going. For example, the Minister of Labour says he is getting a manpower consultant service going. We want to know what the government is going to do about the Hall commission recommendations but we are told, "Just wait until we analyse and get all the facts in." There are committees by the dozen all over the place finding out things, yet here is a government which came to power on a platform that it knew what it was doing.
The minister was a t.v. star, along with the parliamentary secretary to the Minister of

Supply-Defence Production Northern Affairs and National Resources, in those one minute blurbs which were broadcast again and again, in which the main theme was "We know how to get Canada going. We know the answers." I am not going to say any more. Today the minister has revealed he has not got any answers. He is just reading something off, giving details about atomic energy that his civil servants prepared for him. He shows no indication that he has a grasp of this field of science or research. I don't mind him dismissing us as though we did not know anything, but I don't see how a minister, responsible for the field the minister is responsible for, can come into this chamber and treat us so cavalierly and tell us "If you just wait until we get a few more facts and statistics everything will be fine."
I am sorry I have had to express what in effect is a bad temper, but seeing this performance I cannot help but feel we had a giant rooking in the last election campaign and in the general stance of this ministry, which seems to be all-wise and all-knowing.

speakerposition: Minister of Industry; Minister of Defence Production
speechtext:
I do not think I have made claims to be all-wise and all-knowing. If the hon. gentleman asked me what is the policy of the government in relation to science I would say this covers a large field indeed. I am prepared to answer specific questions, but this is a general one. I could answer that the government's policy with regard to science is an approving one; is one of assistance.
Speaking of election campaign undertakings, one of those undertakings was implemented in relation to the proposed appointment of a Canadian science council which, in the scientific field, will perform the same role as the economic council of Canada. It will be the purpose of this body to try and delineate-and I am sure it will be successful -the areas in which scientific endeavour can most usefully be undertaken and those areas in which effort might be less productive than if otherwise employed. This is a step in the organization of the development of science.
If the hon. gentleman has a specific question I would be glad to try and answer it, but to ask what is the policy of the government with relation to science covers a very wide spectrum.
It is your responsibility.

speakerposition: Minister of Industry; Minister of Defence Production
speechtext:
Yes, I agree. It is currently my responsibility and I am prepared, in respect of scientific policy, to give factual answers to the extent that I am able. The hon. gentleman has suggested that the question with


regard to dentistry was brushed off, but if the hon. gentleman had just listened I suggested, as the hon. member for Springfield knows, that there has not been in the dental community the interest and enthusiasm for research that there has been in other fields. Further the medical research council will sympathetically receive applications for assistance in the field of dental research. As far as the medical research council is concerned, there is no shortage of funds or of interest on its side. It is the dental community which has to develop a greater interest in research than it currently possesses.

I wonder if I could ask the minister a question. It is not loaded. If there is a shortage of something obvious, such as librarians or teachers, provincial governments I know of follow a policy of establishing courses to deal with this shortage. In Ontario the provincial government is thinking of establishing a library school. If necessary, teachers colleges are established. In other words, the government accepts responsibility for getting specialists in these fields. But if I understand correctly what the minister is telling the committee, he is really passing the buck-he is passing the whole problem back to the profession. If this is the policy of the government, I am glad to know. The minister has made it perfectly clear. It really means the government has no policy with regard to science or specialties within the field of science; the policy is really one which must be generated within the disciplines themselves. If that is the policy of the government, it is very clear. I do not know whether the hon. member for Springfield received the same impression, but that is what I consider to be a brush-off. I took the minister's answer to be: It is up to the dentists themselves to generate a response.
I just happen to have a different conception of the role of government in the scientific field and all I can do in closing the contribution I am making to this discussion is to suggest that the minister look at some of the papers which have been prepared by the Labour party in Britain, or that he read Mr. Wilson's speech on science. I could also suggest he read a little of C. P. Snow.

I do not wish to become involved in a long debate. However, I cannot accept the minister's proposition that all this money has always been available but there has been nobody to take it. I base this on the fact that the dental profession in Ontario was asked to contribute to a research fund and I think its members did contribute some $50,000.
977a

I am sure they would not have done this if more than enough money was already available for research.
It seems to me that with only one half of 1 per cent of the money going into medical research generally being spent in the field of dentistry, there is an inordinate discrepancy and I believe some initiative should be taken by the national research council to see that it is rectified. The dental profession itself has taken some steps in this regard; it has contributed money to dental research. So, as I say, I cannot accept the proposition that there has been money available which has not been taken up.

speakerposition: Minister of Industry; Minister of Defence Production
speechtext: I would point out that the medical research council does not support dental institutions or organizations. Its help is directed toward individuals, not toward organizations. There are a number of dental organizations across the country which either provide their own funds or which receive assistance from endowments, other bodies such as municipal governments, and so on. The moneys of which I am speaking are the sums available to help highly qualified fellows in the dental field pursue research activities. Obviously the dental associations have projects of their own, both research and performance projects, but the medical research council and, in the wider field, the national research council devote their efforts to individuals rather than to organizations and would not be a source of funds for organizational or institutional activity.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: I should like to ask the minister a question with regard to the annual report of the national research council. The distribution office of the House of Commons has furnished me with the report for the fiscal year 1962-63, the latest one in the possession of that office. Where is the annual report for 1963-64?

speakerposition: Minister of Industry; Minister of Defence Production
speechtext: As on a number of occasions, there has been some difficulty in getting the current report translated, but I am told that it is now in the hands of the printer and we hope it will be available soon.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: We had the same answer from the Minister of Veterans Affairs. This makes two reports which have been very seriously delayed this year.

Very briefly, as we close this discussion, may I say I think the minister was going a long way toward answering our general inquiries to my satisfaction before we were slightly sidetracked. May I assume that the scientific secretariat is making a
Supply-Defence Production study in depth of the reasons for the so-called brain drain and will make recommendations to the minister as to how such a drain can be stopped, if it does exist? Do I understand it will recommend a policy designed to encourage more scientists to stay in Canada and carry out scientific research in Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Industry; Minister of Defence Production
speechtext:
I was about to say with regard to the brain drain that it has been established that over the past six or seven years there has been a net increase of scientists in Canada. The numbers who have been lost either temporarily or permanently by emigration have been more than matched by those gained as a result of immigration. In addition, we have the natural output from our educational institutions. There has also been recently an encouraging return, particularly in a number of medical fields, of senior scientific people from the United States, either Canadians who, having carried out postgraduate work south of the border, return to Canada or of United States citizens who come up here because of the opportunities offered for research work.
It is recognized generally I think-certainly it is recognized by the government-that the scale of research work being carried out in this country is probably not as great as we would like. Consequently, whether or not there is a net brain drain it is desirable to increase the scale of research being done in Canada, and encouragement should be given to this end. The means of encouragement are provided through a number of mechanisms, one of which we have been discussing this afternoon, namely the medical research council. Its appropriations, and consequently its grants, have risen over the current year as compared with the preceding year and are expected to rise again in the coming year. The same is true of the national research council. It is recognized that there should be an increase in the amount of grants made available and we are proposing an increase with a view to lessening whatever net brain drain there may be.
As the hon. member suggested, it is hoped the scientific secretariat will be successful in gathering the basic information upon which an intelligent long range future policy can be based.

One last question. Can it be generally admitted, before we know the findings of the secretariat, that the salaries and remunerations of scientists and the facilities open to them need reconsideration? It seems to me that seven or eight years ago higher salaries and better research facilities per se
9774	HOUSE OF
Supply-Defence Production in the United States seemed to attract our better research brains. They felt it necessary to leave this country in order to work with better facilities in many general fields, and naturally there was talk of higher salaries to a very great extent.
Is it correct to say that in the last few years there has been a general improvement for Canada in this situation? I make these general remarks, Mr. Chairman, realizing that there is a certain amount of folly in preaching nationalism in scientific research, because we have to share our brains with the rest of the world and I do not believe we should always get very excited about our scientists crossing back and forth across the border to the south. But in the two fields I have pinpointed, namely salaries and facilities, has the situation improved considerably in the last year in order to keep Canadian scientists carrying out work in Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of Industry; Minister of Defence Production
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I think I can safely say that both situations have been improved, perhaps to the point now where salary differential is not a significant or too important factor. I am told that what most interests a research scientist are his opportunities to develop his chosen line of research, and that this to him is very much more important-namely the environment in which he works and the kind of work he is doing-than the annual remuneration. So while both have been improved over the past few years, perhaps the more significant is the environment, meaning facilities, than the salary differential.

speechtext: Could we have the minister's estimates brought forward first thing tomorrow and restricted to the questions and answers with regard to the subject we raised this afternoon?

Mr. Chairman, I am sorry that I could not be here earlier, but I think the committee will understand that the foreign minister for Belgium was here. I have just seen him off at the airport. He came specially for a two or three hour visit on a matter of some importance; otherwise I would have been in the chamber this afternoon.
I am in the hands of the house leader. If
he wishes to proceed with the estimates tomorrow, I think that is satisfactory; but I do not know that we should proceed for one purpose: I believe we should proceed to discuss the estimates. Mr. Chairman, I was wondering how much scientific development and research is being undertaken by the department into the problem of the development of industries in underdeveloped areas such as the one I represent; whether any research assistance has been given to this problem, how much, in what areas, and for what purposes?

speakerposition: Minister of Industry; Minister of Defence Production
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, in respect of assistance to underdeveloped areas perhaps some confusion arises in that I am the minister of the Department of Industry whose responsibility it should be, whereas now we are dealing with the national research council, which reports to parliament through me. As the hon. member will recognize, the national research council is not charged with this kind of responsibility. I refer to the development of less favoured areas in Canada. Consequently-

This vote is $300 million and it is authorized for assistance toward research

in industry. I would think that some of this money must be used for the development of industry, if it is authorized; if not, we should know it is not being used.

speakerposition: Minister of Industry; Minister of Defence Production
speechtext: I am not sure what vote the hon. gentleman is now talking about.
I am talking about vote 15(a).

speakerposition: Minister of Industry; Minister of Defence Production
speechtext: That vote, Mr. Chairman, is related to grants made to industrial concerns to assist them in the development of research within the corporate organization. These grants are unrelated to the area in which the industry is operating, but they are made with a view to improving the quality and the quantum of research within a company. They are designed to develop within Canadian industrial organizations a greater ability and a greater talent with which to carry out effective research.

I would assume this to mean that all this money is being used for is to assist industries themselves. Is this the policy of the department? The charge has been made by people that come to my office that if we were to look into the Department of Industry very closely we would find that under the previous deputy minister an immense amount of research and studies was carried out in connection with the aircraft industry, but at the expense of all other sections of research. This may be true, and it may not be true. We are certainly not finding out today. I would think that part of the minister's responsibility should be in respect of those industries that are not as well off as some of those that are able to carry out their own research programs to a degree. I believe some of this vote should be expended in assisting them.
For instance, in my area we have the silver mining industry which has a very great problem in regard to refining. I think development of other industries should take second place to the over-all responsibility for the underdeveloped industrial areas where industrial research could produce industries that would provide employment in the area and do some of the jobs the Department of Industry has so far not been able to do in the underdeveloped areas.
If it is the policy of the department to use this money only to bolster existing industries, then personally I am opposed to it and I think we should reduce the amount. I say this because in my opinion this sum of money could do a great deal of good in areas where we have not been able to develop industries, simply because we do not know what types

We find, for instance, large quantities of slag left in all parts of northern Ontario. Refractory brick, with the proper treatment, could be made from this type of material. We are not capable of doing research in this field. If the national research council is not willing to do it, I ask, who is? The gold mining industry that is leaving the mine is not going to do it, even if it has the money with which to do it. The Department of Industry has to be interested in it, and I think the work has to be done under the national research council. Certainly I am not satisfied that this is being done. I am not satisfied that type of assistance is available.
May I call it six o'clock, Mr. Chairman.

speakerposition: Minister of Industry; Minister of Defence Production
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, if hon. gentlemen are agreeable perhaps I can make a reply to the hon. member's suggestion.
In respect of his specific suggestion about the utilization of slurries, slags and slimeys, this is a field in which the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys has developed very considerable competence and a great deal of skill. It is that department rather than the national research council, which is charged with the responsibility for development in this particular field. It would be inappropriate and perhaps unwise for the national research council, whose estimates we are now considering, because the hon. member does not feel enough is being done, to duplicate or redo the work the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys is doing.
In so far as the second portion of his suggestion is concerned, namely that research money should be expanded in a way to improve the prosperity of small businesses, or in a way to get small businesses established, I should like to point out that research in any field generally calls for an expenditure of something of the order of $30,000 per year per scientist. It is not possible to have any kind of research of a significant character done by much more than a team of three scientists. If we are going to have a coherent and likely productive research effort it calls for a team involving an annual expenditure of something in the order of $90,000 per year. This means that it is very difficult to organize within very small businesses research grants which are going to have a likely and useful productive result. To this end we are trying to encourage industry and the sciences to undertake research work on behalf of all of their constituent members, and thus be
